analysis.one_liner: Requires internet companies to get your permission before using or selling your sensitive personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The CONSENT Act would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring online services like search engines, social media platforms, and streaming services to tell users what sensitive personal data they collect, and to get users' affirmative opt-in consent before using, sharing, or selling that data. It also would have required reasonable data security practices, notice after security breaches, strong protections for de-identified data, and a ban on refusing service to people who decline to consent. It was introduced in May 2018, referred to committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users — anyone with a social media account, search engine, streaming service, or app. The bill treated financial records, health information, children's data, Social Security numbers, precise location, and web browsing history as sensitive data that companies could not use, share, or sell without your explicit opt-in permission. It would also have banned 'take-it-or-leave-it' terms that cut off service to people who refuse to consent, and given state attorneys general power to sue violators on behalf of residents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users and their personal data

how_it_helps.text: Required online platforms to disclose what sensitive data they collect, how they use and share it, and with whom, when a customer signs up and when policies change significantly.

Required opt-in consent before a platform could use, share, or sell sensitive information including financial data, health information, children's data, Social Security numbers, precise location, communications content, and browsing history.
Required the FTC to bar 'take-it-or-leave-it offers' — platforms could not refuse service to a customer who declines to let their data be used for commercial purposes.

Required reasonable data security practices and customer notification after breaches where harm is reasonably likely, and allowed state attorneys general to sue to enforce the rules and obtain damages for residents.

analysis.who_pays: Large internet platforms — search engines, social media companies, streaming services, and app makers — would have borne compliance costs and lost unrestricted access to the user data that fuels targeted advertising. Advertising-driven businesses built on behavioral tracking would have faced the biggest constraints.
analysis.who_pays_short: Search, social media, and streaming platforms

drawbacks.text: Opt-in consent rules impose real compliance costs, which fall hardest on small startups and can push more of the market toward a handful of large companies that can afford the paperwork.

The bill allowed 'pay-for-privacy' arrangements — platforms could offer discounts in exchange for consent to use data, as long as the FTC found the program reasonable and it was fully disclosed — so wealthier users could effectively buy more privacy than others.
Enforcement was left to the FTC and state attorneys general under the FTC Act; the bill contained no private right of action, so individual consumers could not sue violators themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For internet users, the bill would have replaced the current practice — companies quietly harvesting browsing, location, and health-adjacent data under long terms of service — with an affirmative consent requirement, a real gain for privacy. The costs are compliance burdens on platforms, some risk to small competitors, and the concession that discounts could still be traded for data. On balance it was a consumer-protection bill whose main costs fell on the data-harvesting business model.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2018 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Capuano introduced the CONSENT Act in the House on May 15, 2018.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce — the committee with jurisdiction over consumer privacy — and no hearing, markup, or vote followed.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and all legislation not enacted expired; the bill's protections never took effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms and the ad-technology business built on tracking users came out ahead: no consent requirement was imposed, and companies kept collecting and monetizing sensitive personal data under their own terms of service. Internet users gained nothing from this Congress on this issue.

for.name: Rep. Michael Capuano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee; it drew no cosponsors and he did not advance it further before leaving Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over consumer privacy legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 15, 2018 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor action; the bill sat until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no organized opposition — the bill died quietly in committee rather than through a party fight.

industries.industry: Online platforms (search engines, social media, streaming services, app makers)
industries.note: The bill would have required opt-in consent before these companies could use, share, or sell sensitive user data, cutting into the targeted-advertising revenue built on collecting it. The bill's death left their current data practices untouched.
These businesses buy and resell user data from platforms; an opt-in consent mandate would have sharply restricted the supply of data they trade in. With the bill dead, the market continued unchanged.

The bill assigned these already-regulated industries to their existing regulators for enforcement rather than the FTC, adding privacy rules but preserving their current oversight structure. They were not the bill's target.
